transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-10
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Lynx CTO), Priya Rao (Lead ML Eng), Samir Ahmed (Infra Lead), Nora Lin (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hi everybody, thanks for joining, um we got about 45 minutes, I think, hope that works for you all. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on the account.
[00:09] Ethan: Yeah thanks Jordan, thanks Maya. Quick context: Lynx is building a payments risk assistant, multilingual support and strict data residency, we want to understand model options and whether we can run private.
[00:19] Maya: Cool. Quick ask from our side — what are your top success criteria? latency? cost? accuracy? compliance?
[00:26] Nora: All of the above, but top two are compliance (SOC2 + auditable logs) and multilingual accuracy across EN/ES/FR and LatAm Spanish variants. Latency is important but not sub-50ms, more like P95 under 400-500ms for critical flows.
[00:40] Priya: Also, we have long transaction threads and legal notes, so context needs are up to roughly 25k tokens in some cases. That's where the selection challenge is.
[00:52] Samir: One more — we need the option to run in our VPC or on-prem for regulated customers, and keys must be customer-managed via KMS/HSM.
[01:02] Jordan: Understood. So three axes: model capabilities (multilang + long-context), deployment (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and security. We'll try to map models to those needs.
[01:13] Maya: To start, open models: higher flexibility and cost control with quantization, but sometimes tradeoffs on instruction tuning and tool-calling. Closed models (OpenAI/Anthropic) often have stronger baseline safety and function-calling primitives. Are you leaning one way?
[01:27] Ethan: We're cautious about sending PII to third-party hosted APIs without a contract and data residency guarantees, so Private or Dedicated with strict contract is preferable. But we want to see cost math too.
[01:38] Priya: On the model side, we prototyped with an LLaMA-ish 30B quantized model and saw decent multilingual quality but context handling beyond 8k was flaky. We could try some 32k variants or specialized long-context LMs.
[01:52] Maya: Got it. For long context you can: 1) pick a native 32k+ model, 2) use retrieval + shorter context (retrieve relevant chunks), or 3) use KV-prefetch/prefix caching to stitch history. Redwood supports all three patterns — automatic prefix caching and KV cache management.
[02:08] Samir: Wait, KV what?
[02:10] Priya: KV cache, sorry; sometimes the transcriber shows KV cash earlier, but yes the key-value cache, it's the decoder state you can persist so you don't resend entire history.
[02:20] Nora: That sounds promising but how mature is that with open models and quantization?
[02:25] Maya: We're running kernel selection and quantization-friendly paths. Quantizashun does introduce some differences, so we recommend validating on your prompt set. For Dedicated/Private we can enable int8 or awq paths depending on model.
[02:38] Ethan: Tool-calling is also crucial — we need the model to reliably call our payment validation service, KYC lookups, and mask tokens. Does Redwood support function-calling with open models?
[02:49] Jordan: Yes — Redwood has a function/tool-calling surface that works with both hosted and private deployments. For open models we generally route through a shim that maps model outputs to structured calls; SEs implement robust extraction and sanity checks.
[03:01] Priya: Any examples of errors? We saw hallucinated function names and occasionally misformatted JSON from some OSS parsers.
[03:09] Maya: Yeah, that's common. We use a combination of constrained decoding, schema enforcement, and a lightweight verifier layer. For enterprise flows we add an approval step or rule-based fallback.
[03:20] Ethan: On pricing — can you give a rough delta between Hosted (sends to Redwood cloud), Dedicated (reserved GPU pool), and Private (VPC/on-prem) for our expected traffic? We estimate 1.5M tokens/day to start.
[03:35] Jordan: Roughly, hosted is cheapest up-front but with per-token costs and less control; Dedicated gives predictable throughput with a monthly commit (lower costs per token at scale); Private has the highest up-front (deployment, networking, support) but best for data residency and control. I'll follow up with tailored numbers.
[03:50] Samir: For Private, what's the on-prem package look like? Do you ship an appliance or do we run images?
[03:57] Maya: We offer a customer-managed package — container images with an install script, and we support HSM/KMS integration. For very locked-down environments we can do an air-gapped bundle. Maintenance and kernel updates are coordinated with Redwood.
[04:10] Nora: How about model drift and rollouts? We need staged rollouts for a production model swap.
[04:15] Maya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback policies if latency or regression thresholds hit. Logs and token-level traces are available for audits.
[04:25] Priya: Tensor ops — do you support custom kernels if our model has specialized ops?
[04:30] Maya: We can onboard models and contribute compilation paths; for private deployments you can include a custom kernel build as part of the package but that adds ops testing time.
[04:40] Ethan: For multilingual — tokenization differences matter. Our Spanish (LatAm) corpora include some colloquial tokens. How do you evaluate multilingual fidelity?
[04:50] Maya: We run prompt-and-response evals per language using your test set ideally. Redwood Optimize has a model/quantization recommendation engine tuned to workloads; we can profile tokenization breakdowns and show expected token usage per language.
[05:03] Priya: Could you highlight a few candidate open models for us to benchmark? We're looking for 20B-70B parameter ranges but also some efficient 7B variants for chat-ops.
[05:13] Maya: Sure — we usually suggest: 1) An LLM-32k variant (long-context) from the open family for history-heavy flows; 2) A 70B instruction-tuned model for higher accuracy; 3) an efficient 13B/7B quantized model for bursty chat with lower cost. Also compare with Anthropic/Claude and OpenAI gpt-4o-instruct if you want closed models.
[05:33] Samir: Quick Q on latency — with Dedicated GPUs and batching what's typical P95 for a 13B quantized model vs 70B?
[05:40] Maya: Roughly, 13B int8 on a T4 or A10-like class is in the 100-300ms range P95 with modest batch sizes; 70B can be 600-1200ms depending on kernel and sequence length. Exact numbers depend on sequence length and concurrency — we'll benchmark with your prompts.
[05:55] Ethan: Sounds good. About security docs — we'll need SOC2, ISO, and penetration test summaries to share with compliance.
[06:02] Jordan: We'll send our SOC2 report summary and a technical network architecture doc. For Private deployments we provide install network diagrams and audit log configurations.
[06:12] Nora: And SSO? SAML or OIDC?
[06:15] Maya: Both supported — SAML, OIDC, and RBAC role mappings.
[06:19] Priya: For the benchmark we want three lanes: accuracy (multilingual F1 for our intents), latency (P50/P95 for common flows), and cost (tokens/sec and $/1000 tokens).
[06:30] Jordan: That's doable. Maya, will you propose the bench plan?
[06:33] Maya: Yup. I'll include test harness, how to feed prompts (batch vs streaming), and a small runner we can provide. We'll also include retrieval-based experiments, e.g., vector DB + retrieval vs full context.
[06:45] Ethan: Any red flags we should be aware of? Vendor lock-in? Model obsolescence?
[06:50] Jordan: With open models, lock-in is lower but you manage weights. With dedicated/private, you control versions and rollbacks. Redwood's smart routing can also fallback to compatible model variants so you don't go down if capacity is constrained.
[07:02] Priya: We run a regulatory pilot with one financial partner in Q2 and need to be able to prove non-exfiltration and key ownership. That pushes us towards Private but we need to justify cost.
[07:14] Jordan: Agreed. Pilot idea: run a 48-72 hour on-prem benchmark with a subset of real prompts. We can instrument logs and show no payloads leave the VPC.
[07:22] Nora: On instrumentation will logs include token-level redaction and masked PII?
[07:27] Maya: Yes — audit logs can be configured to redact tokens or to store only metadata and hashes. For compliance we can do both and provide an audit trail.
[07:36] Samir: Ok, final question for now — do you support hot-failover to hosted if our private cluster is saturated?
[07:42] Jordan: Yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing: you can prefer private and fallback to dedicated or hosted with masking rules. For strict compliance cases you can disable fallback.
[07:52] Ethan: Alright, summary — we want pricing, SOC2/docation, and a bench plan. We'll share prompt set and evaluate an initial 48-72h private bench.
[07:59] Jordan: Perfect. I'll follow up with the materials. Anything else?
[08:03] Priya: One last note — please include tokenization estimates per language; Spanish tends to use more tokens with our dataset.
[08:09] Maya: Will do.
[08:11] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes and action items.

Meeting recap / closing remarks:
[08:20] Jordan: Recap of next steps: pricing + SOW (Jordan), benchmark plan (Maya), prompt set from Lynx (Priya). Tentatively schedule bench week 2027-01-24.
[08:34] Ethan: Thanks all.
[08:36] Nora: Thanks.
[08:38] Jordan: End.
